mainEntity.name: Is an interim restoration the same as a temporary filling?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not exactly, though the terms are sometimes used interchangeably. A temporary filling typically refers to a material placed within a tooth cavity on a short-term basis — often following root canal treatment or to relieve acute pain. An interim restoration is a broader term that encompasses temporary crowns, bridges, veneers, and other restorative forms, not just fillings. Both serve the purpose of providing short-term protection while a definitive treatment is planned or fabricated.

mainEntity.name: Can an interim restoration fall out, and what should I do?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, interim restorations can become dislodged, particularly if dietary guidance is not followed or if the restoration is subject to excessive force. If your temporary crown or restoration comes loose or falls out, try to avoid chewing on that side and contact your dental practice as soon as possible. In some cases, a dentist may be able to re-cement the same restoration temporarily. Do not attempt to glue the restoration back yourself using household adhesives.

mainEntity.name: Will my interim restoration look natural?

acceptedAnswer.text: Interim restorations in visible areas of the mouth are generally designed to be aesthetically acceptable, but they may not match your natural teeth as precisely as a permanent restoration. Temporary materials are designed for short-term use and may differ in shade, translucency, or shape from your final result. In many cases — particularly during aesthetic treatment planning — interim restorations are used deliberately to preview and refine the final desired appearance before committing to permanent materials.

mainEntity.name: Does wearing an interim restoration hurt?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some sensitivity is common after placement, particularly if the underlying tooth has been prepared or if exposed dentine is present. This usually reduces after a few days. If you experience significant or worsening pain, or if the restoration feels uncomfortable against your bite, you should contact your dental practice. Prolonged or increasing discomfort is worth investigating, as it may indicate an issue with the restoration or the underlying tooth.

mainEntity.name: Can I eat normally with an interim restoration?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can eat, but with some adjustments. Soft foods are recommended, and you should avoid hard, sticky, or chewy items that could dislodge or damage the temporary material. Examples of foods to avoid include chewing gum, toffee, hard bread crusts, raw vegetables, and ice. Eating on the opposite side from the restoration where possible is also advisable. Your dentist will provide specific guidance based on the location and type of interim restoration placed.

mainEntity.name: How will I know when I am ready for a permanent restoration?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your dentist will review your progress at scheduled appointments and determine when conditions are right for the permanent restoration to be placed. For implant cases, this may involve X-rays to assess bone integration. For crown preparation cases, it depends on laboratory timelines and the healing of soft tissue. The transition from interim to permanent restoration is a clinical decision that should not be rushed or delayed unnecessarily.
